stories.title: Impeccable teaches AI agents to have taste in design.
stories.short: Impeccable: design skills for AI agents
stories.dek: A free design vocabulary that stops AI-made interfaces from all looking the same.
stories.body:
Impeccable is an open-source design skills system that gives coding agents a vocabulary for improving interfaces. It started as an extension of Anthropic's frontend design skill and grew into something much bigger.

Inside: 7 reference files (typography, color, spatial, motion, interaction, responsive and UX writing), 23 commands like audit, polish and critique, and 27 rules that catch common design anti-patterns. It works with Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI and other agents that support skills, and it was trending on GitHub with over 32,000 stars.

Paul's point: most models converge on the same look, so if everyone uses the same skill, everything looks alike. Impeccable pushes boldness through hierarchy, scale and decisive typography instead.

discussion.text: Rather than moving directly into code and having no help, they use Impeccable as a bridge, because it communicates the way they communicate.
discussion.author: Paul Bakaus, on Latent Space

stories.why: Proof that a good Claude skill can become a real product. If you design with Claude, you can plug it in today.

stories.title: 20 real things people built with Claude this year.
stories.body:
A countdown of 20 Claude builds from 2026, with the claims checked against the original sources. A few highlights:

• Dave Jones (EEVblog) used Claude to help reverse-engineer firmware for a 121GW multimeter, then tested it on a real meter.
• Nicholas Carlini at Anthropic had 16 agents build a C compiler across nearly 2,000 sessions. The repo warns the code isn't validated.
• Meng To has Claude run a tabletop adventure as game master for his kids.
• Wataru Takasato had Claude write OpenSCAD for a 3D-printed shelf hook. The first print's holes came out too small.
• Austin Lau at Anthropic built a Figma plugin and CSV workflow that turns human-written copy into ad variants.

The lesson the writer draws: the best builds give the agent a concrete job, let it see the result, and test it in the real world.
stories.why: A menu of real, finished things, from silly to serious. Pick one as inspiration for your next weekend build.

stories.title: 48 AI agents searched NASA lidar for lost Maya sites.
stories.body:
Pietro Miotti, a Google engineer and self-described non-archaeologist, turned public NASA lidar scans of about 1,200 km² of Mexican jungle into images. Then 48 agents, run on models including Claude, Gemini and GPT, went through them one by one with a written guide.

They flagged a hilltop with a plaza and an 8 to 12 m oval pyramid, and Mexico's INAH said no site was registered there. The whole thing took under 72 hours.

The twist: the site had already been described in a 2025 archaeology paper the agents missed while searching the literature.
stories.why: Agents are amazing at looking, and still need someone checking the homework.

stories.title: Hacker Times turns Hacker News into a New York Times front page.
stories.body:
Hacker Times takes the firehose of Hacker News and lays it out like a classic newspaper: headlines, deck-style summaries and editorial images instead of a ranked list of links.

In the discussion, one longtime reader said the plain HN interface never gets old and hoped it never changes. Others loved having a calmer way to read the same stories.
stories.why: Same content, completely different feeling. A great lesson in how layout changes how calm reading feels. Sift's close cousin.

stories.title: Blender's famously fast interface, set free.
stories.body:
BUI pulls Blender's famously fast, battery-friendly interface out of Blender and ships it as a small C runtime. You can use it from Python, Rust, JavaScript/React, C, C++ and Dear ImGui.

It includes optional GPU rendering, only redraws what changed, and has an efficient image system. People spent decades polishing Blender's UI, and now anyone can build on it.
stories.why: Interface designers rarely get to borrow a pro tool's UI engine. This makes dense, fast, desktop-grade UI available to anyone.

stories.title: With AI agents everywhere, is Figma in trouble?
stories.body: At Config 2026, Figma put an AI design agent right inside its multiplayer canvas. But the AI powering it comes from providers like Anthropic, who also build competing products such as Claude Design. Figma's answer: human judgment is the part that matters.

views.text: Figma is in a really tough spot right now.
views.author: A Hacker News commenter

views.text: AI is a tool, and the output depends on how you drive it.
views.author: Loredana Crisan, Figma's Chief Design Officer

views.text: Basically anyone who understands systems will be fine and more and more important, even.
views.author: A Hacker News commenter

stories.title: Write a DESIGN.md so every AI tool follows your rules.
stories.short: A DESIGN.md for your AI tools
stories.body:
Google Stitch keeps a project's brand rules, and the reasoning behind them, in a Markdown file called DESIGN.md. Google open-sourced the draft spec in April 2026.

It's the same idea as Impeccable and Claude skills: write your taste down once, and every AI tool you use can follow it.
stories.code:
# DESIGN.md

## Voice
Friendly, plain words. No jargon.

## Color
- Primary #2743E0, for actions only
- Text #121212 on #F7F7F5

## Type
- Headlines: Fraunces 600
- Body: Inter 16px, line height 1.6

## Rules
- Touch targets at least 44px
- One primary button per screen
stories.note: Drop it in your project folder and point Stitch, Claude or any agent at it. These are Sift's own rules, by the way.
stories.why: Five minutes of writing that makes every future AI design session more on-brand.

stories.title: Figma's design agent now works right on the shared canvas.
stories.body:
Figma launched an AI design agent built into its multiplayer canvas. It generates, edits and refines designs alongside the team in real time, and Figma pitches it as a collaborator rather than a chatbot. Weekly users of Figma's MCP server grew fivefold in the first quarter of 2026.

Also new this month: Figma Motion added physics-based springs and a preview of how an animation will play as a Lottie file before you export it.
stories.why: The tool you use every day is changing fast. Worth trying the agent on a real screen this week.

stories.title: The best microscope photo of the year is a printer.
stories.body:
Ole Bielfeldt, a 25-year-old design student in Cologne, Germany, won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a microscope view of an inkjet printer laying ink onto paper. He beat 1,802 entries from 69 countries.

His first tries failed because the printhead moved too fast to stay in focus. So he built his own rig, worked in a dark room and used a flash as his shutter to freeze the droplets mid-air. He says he thought he'd need expensive equipment, and it turned out he already had everything.
stories.why: Curiosity and craft beat budget. A good reminder before you open your design tools today.
